docs.title: Part B: practical task (about 4 hours)
docs.text:
Use a new scenario you have not worked on: for example a retail bank adding an AI loan-assistant for customers in two countries.

  1. Classify the use case under the EU AI Act and list obligations and dates, noting uncertainty (45 minutes).
  2. Draft an obligations register of at least 12 rows across two other jurisdictions (45 minutes).
  3. Write five control objectives and the tests that would prove them (45 minutes).
  4. Write three risk register entries in cause-event-consequence form, with treatment (45 minutes).
  5. Sketch a 90-day plan and the first board decision you would ask for (60 minutes).

docs.text:

Pass mark: 80% of the total on both parts. If you fall short, list your three weakest areas, redo the matching labs, and retake after at least a week.

docs.title: Week 1: Governance fundamentals, inventory and risk tiering
docs.text:
Volume 3 · Weeks 1-2: Governance operating model and global regulation

You will be able to: define who owns AI risk in an organisation, build an AI inventory, and tier use cases by risk so that effort goes where it matters.

Core concepts

  • Why governance exists. AI systems make or shape decisions, learn from data, and change behaviour over time. Governance is the set of roles, rules and evidence that keeps their use accountable, lawful and aligned with the organisation's risk appetite.
  • Roles. Typical roles are a board or executive sponsor, an AI governance committee (security, legal, privacy, risk, data, business), model or system owners, a risk function, and internal audit. Write down who decides, who advises and who is informed for every major decision.
  • Three lines of defence. The first line owns and operates the AI system and its controls. The second line (risk, compliance, security) sets policy and oversees. The third line (internal audit) gives independent assurance.
  • AI inventory. You cannot govern what you have not found. The inventory lists every AI system and use case: owner, purpose, model and vendor, data used, users affected, deployment status and risk tier. Include shadow AI (tools staff use without approval).
  • Use-case intake. A short, mandatory form that new AI uses go through before build or purchase. It feeds the inventory and triggers the right level of review.
  • Risk tiering. Sort use cases into tiers (for example low, medium, high, prohibited) using criteria such as impact on individuals, decision autonomy, data sensitivity, scale, reversibility and regulatory category. Higher tiers get more review, testing and monitoring.

Study plan (about 8 hours)

  1. Read an introductory guide on three lines of defence (any reputable audit-body or risk-framework explanation), about 1.5 hours.
  2. Read the governance sections of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (the "Govern" function) and skim ISO/IEC 42001's management-system structure, about 2.5 hours.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 4 hours.

Guided lab: inventory and tiering for a fictional enterprise

  1. Invent a mid-sized regulated enterprise (for example a regional insurer or logistics company) with at least 12 AI uses: some built in house, some bought, some shadow AI.
  2. Design the inventory as a spreadsheet with the columns above. Fill it in.
  3. Draft a one-page intake form that a business user can complete in ten minutes.
  4. Write a tiering rubric with five to seven criteria, each scored 1-3, and clear tier thresholds. Test it by tiering all your use cases and checking that the results feel defensible. Revise the rubric if two very different uses land in the same tier.
  5. Add your Volume 1 and Volume 2 system as one of the inventory entries, with the red-team findings as risk evidence.

Deliverable (commit to volume3/week1/): the inventory template (populated), the intake form, and the tiering rubric.

Self-check

  1. What does each of the three lines of defence do?
  2. Why does an inventory need to include shadow AI?
  3. Name four criteria you would use to tier an AI use case, and justify one.
  4. What should happen automatically when a use case lands in the highest tier?
  5. Who should approve exceptions to the tiering rules?

docs.title: Week 2: Global regulation and the EU AI Act
docs.text:
Volume 3 · Weeks 1-2: Governance operating model and global regulation

You will be able to: classify AI use cases under the EU AI Act, identify the obligations that follow, and explain which dates currently apply.

Status as of 5 October 2026 (verified from the sources listed at the end; re-check before relying on it)

  • The EU AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. It was amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, signed on 8 July 2026, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and in force from 27 July 2026.
  • The prohibited-practices rules have applied since 2 February 2025, and the obligations for general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers since 2 August 2025.
  • Obligations for stand-alone high-risk systems (Annex III) were deferred from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027. Obligations for AI embedded in products regulated under other EU safety law (Annex I) were deferred to 2 August 2028.
  • Per the sources I read, the Article 50 transparency duties (telling people they are dealing with AI, labelling synthetic content, disclosing deepfakes) were not deferred and apply from 2 August 2026. Some sub-obligations, such as technical marking for systems already on the market, appear to have a later grace date (2 December 2026 in one source). Law-firm summaries vary on how this grace period works, so read the Official Journal text.
  • The Omnibus also adds two new prohibited practices (certain intimate-imagery and child-abuse-material generation) and softens the AI-literacy duty in Article 4 to measures supporting literacy.

Core concepts

  • Risk-based structure. Prohibited practices (banned), high-risk systems (strict obligations), transparency-risk systems (disclosure duties), and minimal-risk systems (no specific obligations). GPAI models have their own obligations.
  • Roles. The Act distinguishes providers (who develop or place a system on the market) from deployers (who use it) and others such as importers and distributors. Your obligations depend on your role.
  • High-risk obligations (when they apply). Risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency to deployers, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, conformity assessment and registration. Read these as a ready-made controls list.
  • Penalties. Per the CSA note I read, up to 35 million euros or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited practices, and up to 15 million euros or 3% for most other violations. Confirm in the regulation text.
  • Beyond the EU. The EU Act is one model among several. Note how other jurisdictions you work in handle AI (voluntary frameworks, sector rules, privacy law) as you reach Weeks 3 and 4.

Study plan (about 8 hours)

  1. Read the Act's structure (recitals skim, then Articles 1-6, 9-15, 26, 50-55, and Annex III) from the official text on EUR-Lex, about 4 hours. You do not need to memorise articles; learn where to look.
  2. Read the CSA research note on the Omnibus (linked in the sources section) and one law-firm summary, about 1.5 hours.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 2.5 hours.

Guided lab: classify ten use cases

For each use case below, decide: prohibited, high-risk, transparency-risk, or minimal; and whether your organisation would be provider or deployer. Write two sentences of reasoning citing the relevant article or annex.

  1. A website chatbot that answers customers' shipping questions.
  2. A tool that ranks job applicants' CVs.
  3. A model that decides consumer-loan eligibility.
  4. An email spam filter.
  5. A government system that scores citizens on social behaviour and restricts their services.
  6. A marketing tool that generates product images.
  7. An AI system that grades exams used for university admission.
  8. A system that infers employees' emotions from webcam video at work.
  9. An internal code assistant used by developers.
  10. Predictive maintenance for factory machinery.

Only after you finish, compare with this indicative key (a teaching answer, not legal advice; edge cases depend on exact facts and the current text): (1) transparency duty to tell users it is AI; (2) high-risk (employment); (3) high-risk (access to essential services); (4) minimal; (5) prohibited; (6) transparency duty for synthetic content; (7) high-risk (education); (8) very likely prohibited in the workplace, with narrow exceptions, so verify against Article 5; (9) minimal for you as a deployer, with obligations falling mainly on the model provider; (10) minimal unless it is a safety component of a regulated product, which would bring Annex I into play.

Deliverable (commit to volume3/week2/): a classification memo of two to three pages with your reasoning for each case, a list of obligations triggered, the dates that apply, and a note of what you are unsure about.

Self-check

  1. What are the four risk categories, and which one carries the heaviest obligations?
  2. What is the difference between a provider and a deployer?
  3. Which obligations did the Omnibus defer, and which did it leave on the original schedule?
  4. Why is it unsafe to rely on a summary of a regulation that is weeks old?
  5. How would a high-risk obligation such as logging map to a technical control you built in Volume 1?

docs.title: Week 3: Frameworks and standards
docs.text:
Volume 3 · Weeks 3-4: Frameworks, standards and regional regulation

You will be able to: explain what each major AI governance framework is for, and cross-map two of them to a single control set.

Core concepts

  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0). A voluntary framework organised around four functions: Govern (culture, roles, policy), Map (context and risks), Measure (assess and track) and Manage (prioritise and treat). A companion Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) applies it to generative AI risks. The curriculum treats both as stable reference documents.
  • ISO/IEC 42001. A certifiable AI management-system standard. Like other ISO management standards, it has requirements on context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement, plus an annex of AI-specific controls. Organisations can be audited against it, which makes it useful for assurance and vendor trust.
  • ISO/IEC 23894. Guidance on AI risk management, aligned with general risk-management principles. Use it to shape your risk process; it is guidance, not a certification scheme.
  • NIST Cyber AI Profile (IR 8596). Per the curriculum, a preliminary draft was published in December 2025 with a later draft expected in summer 2026. I did not verify its current status; check NIST's site.
  • NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative. Per the curriculum, launched in February 2026 (CAISI), with a first interoperability profile planned for Q4 2026 and an NCCoE concept paper on agent identity and authorisation. I did not verify these; check current status.
  • Singapore Model AI Governance Framework. A voluntary, practical framework often cited in Asia and by multinationals. Check which edition and which agentic-AI extension, if any, is current.
  • Other regional instruments. Treat the Saudi, UAE and other ethics principles in Week 4 as inputs to the same crosswalk.

Study plan (about 8 hours)

  1. Read the NIST AI RMF core (functions and categories) and skim AI 600-1's list of generative-AI risks, about 3 hours.
  2. Read a good summary of ISO/IEC 42001's structure, and the standard itself if you have access through your organisation or library, about 2 hours. ISO standards are paid documents; do not copy their text into your portfolio.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 3 hours.

Guided lab: one control set, two frameworks

  1. Choose two frameworks, for example NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001.
  2. Write your own control set of 15 to 25 control objectives in your own words. Group them under headings such as governance and accountability, inventory and classification, data governance, model lifecycle, testing and validation, security, transparency and human oversight, third-party risk, monitoring and incidents.
  3. Map each control objective to the relevant function or clause in each framework. Mark strong, partial or no coverage.
  4. Add a column linking each control to the Volume 1 or 2 evidence (a test, a finding, a configuration) that would show it works.
  5. Identify gaps: frameworks' topics your control set misses, and control objectives no framework covers.

Deliverable (commit to volume3/week3/): the framework crosswalk as a spreadsheet, plus a half-page note on what each framework is best suited for.

Self-check

  1. What are the four functions of the NIST AI RMF?
  2. What is the difference between ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC 23894?
  3. Why would an organisation pursue ISO/IEC 42001 certification, and what does certification not guarantee?
  4. Why write your own control set instead of adopting one framework verbatim?
  5. Which draft or fast-moving items in this week would you re-check before a client meeting?

docs.title: Week 4: Regional regulation: GCC and India
docs.text:
Volume 3 · Weeks 3-4: Frameworks, standards and regional regulation

You will be able to: build a multi-jurisdiction obligations register for a single AI use case and mark how sure you are of each entry.

Read this first. The table below is a snapshot as of 5 October 2026 from the sources listed at the end. Items marked "verified in sources" were found in documents I opened or in multiple search results; items marked "not verified" are things I could not confirm. All of it needs checking against official texts and local counsel before use.

Jurisdiction What I found Confidence India The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and the DPDP Rules 2025 were notified on 13 November 2025 and commence in three phases. Institutional provisions (including the Data Protection Board) started then; the consent-manager framework starts on 13 November 2026; the main obligations (notice, consent, rights, security safeguards, breach handling, children's data, penalties) start 18 months after notification, on or about 13 May 2027. Sources differ by a day (12 or 13 May), so check the notification Verified in sources (law-firm summaries; read the Gazette notification) UAE (federal) The Personal Data Protection Law is Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021. A June 2026 law-firm note states its implementing regulations had still not been issued and that no private-sector supervisor was clearly designated. On 14 June 2026 the UAE announced a Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data to consolidate AI, data and digital-government functions. One lower-quality web source claims the regulations have since been issued; I could not corroborate that Partly verified: re-check whether implementing regulations exist now UAE free zones DIFC and ADGM have their own data-protection regimes and active regulators, independent of the federal law. DIFC has additional rules on autonomous and semi-autonomous systems (I recall a "Regulation 10"; verify) Partly verified Saudi Arabia The Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19) came into force on 14 September 2023, with enforcement after a one-year transition from mid-September 2024, with implementing and transfer regulations. SDAIA's AI Ethics Principles (September 2023) and Generative AI Guidelines (January 2024) are soft law. Sources I saw say there is no dedicated AI law yet, though a draft Global AI Hub Law was reported in April 2025 and a dedicated AI law is widely expected. Reports also describe an SDAIA AI Adoption Framework for public bodies (late 2025) Mostly from search summaries; verify Oman A personal-data-protection law exists Not verified in this revision: confirm the current law, executive regulations and effective dates

Core concepts

  • Personal data law is the practical AI law in this region. Where no AI-specific statute exists, training, fine-tuning and using a model on personal data falls under data-protection duties: lawful basis or consent, purpose limitation, minimisation, security, cross-border transfer conditions, data-subject rights and breach duties.
  • Soft law still matters. Ethics principles and government frameworks are often written into tenders, procurement and sector regulator expectations, so they behave like requirements in practice.
  • Cross-border data and cloud AI. Sending prompts or documents to a model hosted abroad can be a cross-border transfer. Map where inference, logging and vendor support happen.
  • Sector regulators add duties. Financial regulators, health authorities and critical-infrastructure authorities issue their own AI and cyber rules. Add them if the use case is in a regulated sector.
  • Uncertainty is a finding. In a register, "status unclear, owner to confirm by date" is a legitimate and honest entry.

Study plan (about 8 hours)

  1. Read the official text of the DPDP Act and Rules, focusing on obligations of data fiduciaries and the phasing, about 2.5 hours.
  2. Read the UAE and Saudi data-protection laws at article-heading level, plus SDAIA's AI Ethics Principles, about 3 hours.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 2.5 hours.

Guided lab: an obligations register

  1. Pick one AI use case: a customer-support assistant that uses retrieval over customer records, serving customers in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, India and the EU, hosted by a cloud provider outside those regions.
  2. For each jurisdiction, list every obligation you can find that touches the use case: consent or lawful basis, transparency, rights, security, breach reporting, transfer rules, AI-specific duties, sector rules.
  3. For each row record: obligation, source (law and article), applies from (date), status (in force, phased, draft, unclear), the control that satisfies it (from your Week 3 control set), the owner, and a confidence rating.
  4. Mark every "unclear" and write the question for counsel.
  5. Highlight overlaps. One control, such as breach notification, may satisfy several rows.

Deliverable (commit to volume3/week4/): the obligations register with at least 25 rows, an "open questions for counsel" list, and a one-page summary of overlaps and the strictest common standard.

Self-check

  1. Why is personal-data law central to AI compliance in jurisdictions without an AI statute?
  2. What are India's three DPDP commencement stages?
  3. Why can a prompt sent to an offshore model be a regulated transfer?
  4. Why must you record the date and source for every legal claim?
  5. When is "unclear" the right answer in a register?

docs.title: Week 5: Policy stack, control objectives and the risk register
docs.text:
Volume 3 · Weeks 5-6: Policy, risk register and third-party risk

You will be able to: write a coherent set of AI policies, link them to testable control objectives, and maintain a risk register that decision-makers can use.

Core concepts

  • The policy stack. Layers from broad to specific. A top-level AI governance policy sets principles, roles and scope. Beneath it sit focused policies: acceptable use of AI (including generative AI and shadow AI), model lifecycle (build, validate, deploy, retire), data used for AI, third-party AI, and AI incident management. Below policies sit standards and procedures that say exactly how.
  • Control objectives. A policy statement says what must be true ("AI systems that process personal data must have a documented lawful basis"). A control objective restates it as something you can test. Controls are the mechanisms that achieve it.
  • AI impact assessments. A structured review of an AI use case's effects on individuals, the organisation and society. Many privacy laws require data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing; an AI impact assessment can build on that work instead of duplicating it. Design one form that satisfies both where possible.
  • Risk register. A living list of risks with owner, likelihood, impact, existing controls, residual risk, treatment decision and review date. Write each risk as cause, event and consequence, not as a vague label such as "bias".
  • Treatment options. Mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept. Acceptance needs a named senior owner and a review date.
  • Linking technical evidence. Your Volume 2 findings are risk inputs. A prompt-injection finding with a measured success rate is stronger evidence than a general statement that injection is possible.

Study plan (about 8 hours)

  1. Read two or three published organisational AI policies or templates from reputable bodies (search for current public examples), noting structure and length, about 2 hours.
  2. Read the risk-assessment sections of the NIST AI RMF and the ISO/IEC 23894 summary, about 2 hours.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 4 hours.

Guided lab: policy pack and populated risk register

  1. Draft a pack for your fictional enterprise: a top-level policy (two pages), an acceptable-use policy (two pages), a model lifecycle policy (two to three pages) and an AI impact assessment form (two pages).
  2. For each policy, extract at least five control objectives and link them to your Week 3 control set.
  3. Build a risk register with at least 15 entries covering the system you built in Volumes 1 and 2. Include risks such as prompt injection, data leakage through retrieval, over-privileged agent actions, model-supply-chain compromise, regulatory non-compliance, and vendor lock-in.
  4. For each entry, rate inherent risk, list controls, rate residual risk, and decide treatment. Where a Volume 2 finding exists, cite it.
  5. Review the register for two entries that you rated too optimistically. Explain what evidence would change the rating.

Deliverable (commit to volume3/week5/): the policy pack and the populated risk register.

Self-check

  1. What is the difference between a policy, a standard and a procedure?
  2. How does a control objective differ from a policy statement?
  3. Rewrite "AI bias" as a properly framed risk (cause, event, consequence).
  4. Who may accept a high residual risk, and what must accompany that decision?
  5. How can one assessment serve both a privacy impact assessment and an AI impact assessment?

docs.title: Week 6: Third-party and vendor AI risk
docs.text:
Volume 3 · Weeks 5-6: Policy, risk register and third-party risk

You will be able to: run a structured due-diligence and evaluation of an AI vendor, from questionnaire to proof of concept and contract.

Core concepts

  • Why vendor AI risk differs. You inherit risks you cannot inspect: training data provenance, model behaviour changes without notice, sub-processors, retention of your prompts, and weak security of the vendor's own platform.
  • Due diligence. Questions on security certifications and audits, data handling and retention, whether your data trains their models, sub-processors and hosting locations, incident history and notification terms, model change management, and exit and portability.
  • Model cards and system documentation. Request them. A vendor who cannot explain intended use, limitations and evaluation results is a risk signal.
  • AI bill of materials (AI-BOM). An inventory of the models, datasets, libraries and services in an AI system, extending the SBOM idea from Volume 1.
  • Contract clauses. Data use limits, confidentiality, audit rights, breach notification timelines, sub-processor approval, service levels, change notification for models, indemnities, exit assistance and data deletion.
  • Shadow-AI discovery. Find unapproved tools through network telemetry, browser extensions, expense reports and staff surveys. Then offer a sanctioned alternative; bans alone push usage underground.
  • RFP and proof of concept. In an RFP, define requirements, weights and mandatory gates. In a proof of concept, test the vendor's claims against your own scenarios, including security tests from Volume 2. Score using the weights you fixed in advance.

Study plan (about 8 hours)

  1. Read vendor-risk guidance from a recognised source on third-party risk management, plus sample AI vendor questionnaires published by reputable organisations (search for current ones), about 2.5 hours.
  2. Read the data-processing and AI-related terms of one real vendor's public documentation (for example a cloud AI service's data-use page), about 1.5 hours.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 4 hours.

Guided lab: score two vendors

  1. Define a requirement: for example an AI document-summarisation service for confidential customer contracts.
  2. Build a weighted evaluation framework with six to eight categories. Suggested categories: security and certifications, data protection and residency, model governance and transparency, AI-specific security controls, resilience and exit, regulatory fit, commercial terms, support. Set weights that total 100 and define 1-5 scoring anchors before you score.
  3. Make two fictional vendor profiles with different strengths. Score them. Identify mandatory gates (for example "customer data is never used to train models") and show how a gate failure disqualifies a vendor regardless of total score.
  4. Write the proof-of-concept test plan: at least five tests, including one prompt-injection test, one data-leakage test and one access-control test, each with pass/fail criteria.
  5. Draft a one-page clause checklist for the contract.

Deliverable (commit to volume3/week6/): a vendor evaluation workbook with weights, scores, gates, PoC test plan and clause checklist.

Self-check

  1. Why should evaluation weights and scoring anchors be fixed before vendors are scored?
  2. What is an AI-BOM and what questions does it help answer?
  3. Name four contract clauses specific to AI services.
  4. How does shadow-AI discovery work, and why is banning not enough?
  5. Which Volume 2 techniques belong in a vendor proof of concept?

docs.title: Week 7: Audit, assurance and monitoring
docs.text:
Volume 3 · Weeks 7-8: Assurance, monitoring and the capstone

You will be able to: test whether AI controls work, gather and document evidence, define useful indicators, and judge readiness for an ISO/IEC 42001 audit.

Core concepts

  • Assurance versus compliance. Compliance asks whether a rule exists and was followed. Assurance asks whether you can show, with evidence, that controls are designed well and operating effectively.
  • Control testing. Two questions per control: is it designed to address the risk (design effectiveness), and does it work in practice over time (operating effectiveness)? Methods include inquiry, inspection of documents, observation, re-performance and technical testing.
  • Evidence. Reliable evidence is specific, dated, attributable and reproducible. Screenshots with no date and policies with no sign-off are weak. Logs, configuration exports, test outputs and approvals are strong.
  • Sampling. You rarely test everything. State the population, the sample method and the sample size, and say what the sample can and cannot tell you.
  • KRIs and KPIs. Key risk indicators warn that risk is rising (for example, share of AI systems without an owner, rate of failed guardrail checks, number of shadow-AI tools detected). Key performance indicators show the programme is working (for example, percentage of use cases assessed before launch). Each indicator needs a definition, a data source, a threshold and an owner.
  • Incident reporting and continuous monitoring. Define what counts as an AI incident (harmful output, data leak, model drift beyond a threshold, unauthorised agent action), who is told, how fast, and what regulators or customers must be notified. Monitor models and controls continuously; one audit per year is not enough for systems that change.
  • ISO/IEC 42001 readiness. A readiness review checks scope, documented information, internal audit, management review and corrective action. Use it as a gap assessment before inviting a certification body.

Study plan (about 8 hours)

  1. Read an introduction to internal-audit practice (planning, fieldwork, working papers, reporting) from a recognised audit body, about 2 hours.
  2. Review ISO/IEC 42001's management-review and internal-audit requirements through a summary or the standard itself, about 1.5 hours.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 4.5 hours.

Guided lab: audit your own system

  1. Select 10 controls from your Week 3 control set that apply to the Volume 1 system.
  2. For each control, write a test: what you will inspect or run, what counts as pass, and the sample.
  3. Run the tests. Use real artefacts from your repository: CI results, access-control tests, logs, Volume 2 retests, configuration files.
  4. Record each result in a working-paper format: control, test performed, evidence reference, result (effective, partly effective, ineffective), observations.
  5. Write findings for each failure or weakness with root cause, risk, recommendation, owner and target date.
  6. Define six indicators (three KRIs, three KPIs) with thresholds and data sources.

Deliverable (commit to volume3/week7/): audit working papers, findings, and the indicator set.

Self-check

  1. What is the difference between design effectiveness and operating effectiveness?
  2. Give two examples of strong and two of weak evidence for an access-control test.
  3. What makes a good KRI?
  4. What would you include in an AI incident definition?
  5. What does an ISO/IEC 42001 readiness review check, and what happens next if gaps are found?

docs.title: Week 8: Capstone: a governance programme for a regulated enterprise
docs.text:
Volume 3 · Weeks 7-8: Assurance, monitoring and the capstone

You will be able to: design, justify and present an AI governance programme that a board can approve.

The brief

The curriculum asks you to design an AI governance programme for a regulated enterprise and present it to a simulated board. Choose one from a list that interests you or that matches your career target: a bank, an insurer, a hospital group, a government agency, an airline or a telecom operator. Give it a realistic size, geography (include at least two jurisdictions from Week 4) and a portfolio of 10 to 15 AI use cases, including at least one agentic use case.

What to deliver

  1. Programme charter. Purpose, scope, principles, governance bodies, decision rights, and escalation paths.
  2. Operating model. Roles, three-lines responsibilities, a committee calendar, and the intake-to-retirement lifecycle for an AI use case.
  3. Inventory and tiering result. Your Week 1 artefacts applied to the chosen enterprise.
  4. Regulatory map. A summary of the obligations register, with dates, owners and confidence levels.
  5. Policy and control set. The policy stack and the control objectives it implies.
  6. Risk picture. The top ten risks with ratings, treatments and indicators.
  7. Assurance plan. What is tested, how often, and by whom.
  8. Roadmap. A phased plan over 12 to 24 months with milestones, owners, rough resource needs and dependencies. Show what happens in the first 90 days.
  9. Board presentation. Eight to ten minutes, five slides at most: why it matters, what we do, what it costs and delivers, the risks and decisions needed, the asks.

Study plan (about 8 hours)

  1. Read two examples of board-level reports on technology or cyber risk, noting how they frame decisions, about 1.5 hours.
  2. Plan and assemble the capstone, about 6.5 hours. Expect to extend into a second week.

Quality checks before you present

  • Every claim about a law or standard cites its source and a date.
  • Every top risk links to evidence or a clearly labelled assumption.
  • The roadmap shows trade-offs and what you are deliberately not doing.
  • Someone outside the field could say what decision you want from the board.

Deliverable (commit to volume3/week8/): the programme pack, the roadmap, and the board presentation with speaker notes. This is your Volume 3 gate artefact.

Self-check

  1. What decisions do you need from the board, and what happens if they say no?
  2. What are the first three things you would do in the first 90 days?
  3. Which part of your programme depends most on regulation that may change, and how will you handle that?
  4. How will you know in a year that the programme is working?
  5. What would an auditor challenge first in your pack?

docs.title: Volume 4: Secure AI Architecture and Engineering
docs.text:
Volume 4 is the architect core of the programme: 8 weeks, about 80 hours by the curriculum's planning estimate, roughly 10 hours a week. You take everything you learned and fix the system you built in Volume 1 properly.

You return to the same system, now with known weaknesses from Volume 2 and known obligations from Volume 3. The question changes from "how does it break?" to "what design would have prevented or contained this, and how do I prove it works?". The volume ends with a capstone: an integrated package for a secure agentic AI platform, defended in front of a design-authority panel.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Volumes 1 to 3, or equivalent. Experienced governance learners may run Volume 3 in parallel, as the curriculum allows.
  • Your portfolio repository containing: the RAG app, agent and MCP server (V1), the threat model (V1), the red-team report and findings (V2), the control set, risk register and obligations register (V3).
  • The lab from earlier volumes: Docker, Python, Git, a local model server, Kubernetes via kind or minikube.

docs.title: Weekly rhythm (about 10 hours)
docs.text: Block Hours What you do Learn 3 Study the week's patterns, standards and vendor-neutral references Design 2 Produce the architecture decisions and diagrams for the week Build 4 Implement and test the lab changes on your Volume 1 system Check 1 Self-check questions, closed-book

docs.title: How you document architecture in this volume
docs.text:
Every week produces design artefacts in the same shape, so the capstone is assembled from weekly parts.

Artefact What it must contain Context and component diagram Components, data flows, trust boundaries, identities. Use a tool you like (Mermaid, draw.io, Excalidraw) and keep the source in Git Threat model Assets, entry points, threats (STRIDE or an agent-specific method), existing controls, gaps Architecture decision record (ADR) Context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences, status, date. One page each Control mapping Which control objective from your Volume 3 control set each design element satisfies Test evidence The test, tool or measurement that shows the control works, with results Residual risk What remains after the design, who accepts it, and a review date

docs.title: Principles to apply every week
docs.text:
• Reduce capability before adding filters. A tool the agent does not have cannot be abused.
  • Assume the model can be manipulated. Place enforcement outside the model, in code and infrastructure.
  • Least privilege everywhere, including the identities of agents and tools.
  • Defence in depth with independent layers. One bypass should not defeat everything.
  • Design for observability and for stopping. If you cannot see it or switch it off, you do not control it.
  • Prove it. A design claim without a test is only a hope.

docs.title: Self-grading
docs.text: The curriculum expects 80% or higher on the gate and a successful capstone defence. Score artefacts against the rubric at the end of the volume.

docs.title: Volume 4 gate
docs.text:
Volume 4 Gate and programme assessment

The curriculum's gate output for this volume is an architecture package plus a live design-authority defence. The final programme decision depends on all four gates and the capstone.

docs.title: Part A: closed-book exam (about 40 questions)
docs.text:
Build the questions from your weekly self-checks, answer without notes, then mark honestly.

Area Weeks Questions What to cover Reference architectures and threat modelling 1 6 Five patterns, STRIDE, ADRs, trust boundaries Data and RAG security 2 6 Permission-aware retrieval, identity source, tenant isolation, PII, lineage Model and supply-chain security 3 6 Provenance, safe formats, signing, AI-BOM, intake gates Guardrails and runtime protection 4 6 Gateway, layered checks, block versus false-positive rates, policy engines Agent and MCP security 5 8 Identity, scoped tools, approvals, sandboxing, kill switches Detection and response 6 5 Telemetry, detections, playbooks, containment Enterprise architecture and business case 7 3 Hosting options, risk quantification, roadmap

docs.title: Part B: practical design review (about 4 hours)
docs.text:
You are given a description of a new system you have not seen (write one for yourself, or have a friend write it): for example, an AI assistant for a hospital that reads patient notes and can book appointments.

  1. Produce a context diagram with trust boundaries (45 minutes).
  2. List the top ten threats, mapped to components (45 minutes).
  3. Propose controls for the top five and say how you would test each (60 minutes).
  4. Write two ADRs for the hardest decisions (45 minutes).
  5. Identify the three biggest residual risks and what you would ask the owner to accept or fund (45 minutes).

docs.title: Week 1: Secure AI reference architectures and threat modelling
docs.text:
Volume 4 · Weeks 1-2: Reference architectures, threat modelling, data and RAG security

You will be able to: describe the standard AI system patterns, threat-model them with STRIDE and an agent-specific method, and record your decisions as ADRs.

Core concepts

  • Five patterns to know. Each has a different trust profile.
    • LLM application: user, application, model API, optional tools. Main concerns: prompt injection, output handling, data sent to the model.
    • RAG: adds a retrieval layer and a knowledge base. Main concerns: who can write to the corpus, who can read from it, and untrusted retrieved text.
    • Agent: the model chooses actions through tools. Main concerns: excessive agency, identity, approvals, and runaway loops.
    • Multi-agent: several agents exchange messages. Main concerns: trust between agents, spoofing, cascading failure.
    • MLOps pipeline: data, training, registry, deployment, monitoring. Main concerns: data and model integrity, supply chain, secrets, access to training infrastructure.
  • STRIDE. A checklist for threats to each component and data flow: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. It works well for the conventional parts of an AI system and still applies to AI components.
  • Agent-specific methods. The curriculum names the Cloud Security Alliance's MAESTRO framework as an example of a layered method for agentic systems. I have not verified its current version, so read the CSA's current publication and use whichever agent-aware method your organisation prefers.
  • Architecture decision records. Short documents that capture why a design choice was made. They stop decisions being re-litigated and help auditors and successors.
  • Trust boundaries again. Mark where data crosses from untrusted to trusted, where identity changes, and where the model's output becomes an action.

Study plan (about 10 hours)

  1. Read a STRIDE tutorial from a recognised source and review OWASP's guidance on threat modelling, about 2 hours.
  2. Read the current CSA material on agentic threat modelling and the OWASP LLM and Agentic lists again, now as a designer, about 3 hours.
  3. Read two or three published ADR examples, about 1 hour.
  4. Lab and deliverable, about 4 hours.

Guided lab: baseline the insecure system

  1. Draw the Volume 1 system as it currently exists: browser or client, API, RAG pipeline, vector store, model server, agent, MCP server, logging, identities. Show data flows with arrows and mark every trust boundary.
  2. Run STRIDE on each component and each flow. Add the agent-specific threats from Volume 2 (goal hijack, tool misuse, memory poisoning, over-broad identity).
  3. Merge in your Volume 2 findings. Each confirmed finding becomes a threat with evidence.
  4. Rank the threats by risk, using your Volume 3 rating scheme.
  5. Write three ADRs for decisions you already know you must make: for example "Where will authorisation be enforced?", "Will the model be allowed to call tools directly?", "Where will the model be hosted?".

Deliverable (commit to volume4/week1/): the baseline architecture diagram, the threat model, and three ADRs. This baseline is what you will improve and compare against for the rest of the volume.

Self-check

  1. What does each letter of STRIDE represent? Give an AI example for two of them.
  2. Why does an agent change the threat model compared with a plain chatbot?
  3. What makes a good ADR?
  4. Where does the model's output become an action in your system?
  5. Which of your baseline threats has the weakest existing control?

docs.title: Week 2: Securing data and RAG
docs.text:
Volume 4 · Weeks 1-2: Reference architectures, threat modelling, data and RAG security

You will be able to: enforce who can retrieve what, reduce exposure of personal data, and prove it with the attacks you ran in Volume 2.

Core concepts

  • Data classification. Label data (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) so that controls can depend on it. Classification travels with the data into chunks and embeddings.
  • Permission-aware retrieval. Access control must be applied at retrieval time, using the caller's verified identity. Good practice is to store access metadata with every chunk at ingestion, filter inside the vector query, and re-check before passing text to the model.
  • Identity must not come from the prompt. A user's claim in a chat message ("I am the finance director") is not an identity. Take identity from the authenticated session or token and pass it to the retrieval layer yourself.
  • Vector database security. Authentication, network isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, per-tenant separation (separate collections, namespaces or indexes), backups, and audit logs. Remember that embeddings can leak information about the original text.
  • Tenant isolation. Prefer strong separation (distinct stores or collections per tenant) over a single shared index with filters when the stakes are high. If you share an index, test the filter exhaustively.
  • PII handling. Detect and redact or tokenise personal data before indexing where it is not needed, and again on the way out to the user and to logs. Detection is imperfect; combine it with data minimisation.
  • DLP and output controls. Scan model outputs for secrets and personal data, block or mask, and log the event.
  • Data lineage. Track where each document came from, who approved it, when it was ingested and which models used it. Lineage supports deletion requests and incident response.

Study plan (about 10 hours)

  1. Read your vector store's documentation on metadata filtering and access control, about 2 hours.
  2. Read guidance on PII detection and anonymisation techniques and their limits (for example, the documentation of an open-source tool such as Microsoft Presidio; check its current docs), about 2 hours.
  3. Review the data-protection duties you recorded in your Volume 3 obligations register, about 1 hour.
  4. Lab and deliverable, about 5 hours.

Guided lab: harden the RAG pipeline

  1. Add an authentication layer to the RAG API so every request carries a verified user identity and roles. Use a simple token scheme for the lab.
  2. At ingestion, attach classification and allowed-roles metadata to every chunk. Add provenance fields (source, owner, ingest time).
  3. At query time, filter by the caller's roles inside the vector query. Add a second check on the retrieved set before it reaches the prompt.
  4. Add PII detection and redaction at ingestion and on outputs. Measure how many seeded fake personal records slip through.
  5. Rerun your Volume 2 Week 5 attacks: cross-department canaries, cross-tenant tests, poisoning with a hidden instruction. Record before and after leakage rates.
  6. Write an ADR for your tenant-isolation choice and a short note on what the design still does not protect against.

Deliverable (commit to volume4/week2/): the hardened RAG design, the code changes and tests, and a before-and-after table of attack results.

Self-check

  1. Why must access control be enforced at retrieval time and not only at ingestion?
  2. Why can the user's identity never come from the prompt?
  3. When would you choose per-tenant collections over a shared index with filters?
  4. What are the limits of PII redaction, and what complements it?
  5. How does lineage help when a user asks you to delete their data?

docs.title: Week 3: Securing models and the AI supply chain
docs.text:
Volume 4 · Weeks 3-4: Models, supply chain, guardrails and runtime protection

You will be able to: design a gated pipeline that brings models into your environment safely and keeps track of what is running where.

Core concepts

  • Provenance. Know where a model came from: publisher, repository, version, hash, licence, training-data claims and any fine-tuning applied. Unknown provenance is a risk factor in itself.
  • Safe formats. Prefer formats that store only tensors and cannot execute code on load (as you saw in Volume 2 Week 7). Where a pickle-based file is unavoidable, load it only in an isolated sandbox.
  • Scanning gates. Scan model files and dependencies for known-unsafe constructs and vulnerabilities before admission. No scanner is complete, so a scan is one gate among several.
  • Signing and verification. Cryptographic signatures let a consumer verify that an artefact came from a known builder and was not altered. General-purpose tools such as Sigstore's Cosign can sign arbitrary files; the OpenSSF community also works on model-specific signing. Check current documentation and maturity before depending on either.
  • AI-BOM. A bill of materials listing models, datasets, libraries, containers and services in each AI system, with versions and hashes. It answers "are we affected?" when a new vulnerability or licence problem appears.
  • Registry and promotion. Keep approved models in an internal registry with access control. Promote through stages (candidate, tested, approved, production) with recorded approvals.
  • Fine-tuning data governance. Fine-tuning data needs the same controls as production data: classification, consent or lawful basis, quality checks for poisoning, and retention rules. Check that sensitive data did not enter training sets.
  • Sovereign and on-premises hosting. Regulated or sensitive workloads may require that models and data stay within a country or an organisation. Weigh control and residency against cost, capability and the burden of patching and operating GPU infrastructure yourself.

Study plan (about 10 hours)

  1. Read supply-chain security guidance such as the SLSA framework overview and the documentation of your chosen signing tool, about 3 hours.
  2. Review your Volume 2 Week 7 assessment report and your Volume 3 vendor workbook, about 1 hour.
  3. Read about sovereign or in-country AI hosting considerations for a region you care about, about 1.5 hours.
  4. Lab and deliverable, about 4.5 hours.

Guided lab: a model-intake pipeline

  1. Define the pipeline stages on paper: request, provenance check, licence check, download to quarantine, format check, scan, sandbox load and behavioural smoke test, sign, register, approve, deploy.
  2. Implement as many stages as you can as scripts or a CI workflow: hash verification, a scan step, a rule that rejects non-safe formats, signing and verifying an artefact, and generating an AI-BOM entry.
  3. Test the pipeline with three artefacts: a good one, one that fails a gate (for example a wrong hash), and your harmless Volume 2 pickle test file, which must be rejected.
  4. Write the model-intake policy that the pipeline enforces, linked to your Volume 3 control objectives.
  5. Write an ADR on hosting (cloud-managed, self-hosted in cloud, or on-premises) with at least three alternatives compared.

Deliverable (commit to volume4/week3/): the model-intake policy and pipeline, test results for the three artefacts, an AI-BOM sample, and the hosting ADR.

Self-check

  1. What does a signature prove about a model file and what does it not?
  2. Why is scanning insufficient on its own?
  3. What question does an AI-BOM help you answer during an incident?
  4. What extra risks come with fine-tuning data?
  5. What are the trade-offs of on-premises hosting for a regulated workload?

docs.title: Week 4: Guardrails, runtime protection and vendor evaluation
docs.text:
Volume 4 · Weeks 3-4: Models, supply chain, guardrails and runtime protection

You will be able to: place layered runtime controls around a model, measure what they catch and what they wrongly block, and decide between building and buying.

Core concepts

  • Where controls sit. Input filters, retrieval filters, the model, output filters, tool-call checks and logging. Each layer sees different information; none is sufficient alone.
  • AI gateway. A single entry point between applications and models. It centralises authentication, rate limits, quotas, logging, prompt and response inspection, model routing and policy. It also gives you one place to switch things off.
  • Guardrail approaches. Rule-based checks (patterns, allow-lists), classifiers (models trained to detect injection, toxicity or leaks), and structural checks (schema validation, canary detection). Open-source examples include LLM Guard, NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails and Meta's Llama Guard; check each one's current status, scope and licence.
  • Policy engines. Systems such as Open Policy Agent let you write access and action rules as code, evaluate them outside the model, and test them like software.
  • Measuring guardrails. Block rate on attacks (from your Volume 2 suite) and false-positive rate on legitimate traffic. A guardrail that blocks 99% of attacks and 20% of normal requests is rarely acceptable. Report both with sample sizes.
  • AI security vendors. The market includes products for discovering AI usage and posture (often called AI security posture management, AI-SPM), runtime protection and red-teaming. The category changes quickly with acquisitions and rebranding; evaluate by capability, not by label.
  • Build versus buy. Consider coverage, integration effort, accuracy on your traffic, data handling and residency, lock-in, total cost and your team's ability to run it.

Study plan (about 10 hours)

  1. Read the documentation of two guardrail tools and one policy engine, about 3 hours.
  2. Reread your Volume 3 Week 6 vendor-evaluation method, about 1 hour.
  3. Skim current analyst or independent comparisons of AI runtime-protection categories (search for recent, non-promotional sources and note dates), about 1.5 hours.
  4. Lab and deliverable, about 4.5 hours.

Guided lab: gateway and guardrails

  1. Put a simple gateway in front of your model: a small service that authenticates callers, logs each call, enforces rate limits and applies checks.
  2. Add layered checks: input screening, output scanning for canaries and personal data, and schema validation. Keep each layer separately switchable so you can measure it.
  3. Build a test set: your Volume 2 attack suite (at least 50 attack prompts) and 200 benign prompts that resemble real use.
  4. Measure for each layer and for the combined stack: attack block rate, false-positive rate and added latency. Find the weakest attack class.
  5. Add one policy-as-code rule outside the model, for example "the agent may not call the ticket tool for customers outside its assigned region", and test it.
  6. Write a build-versus-buy memo for the runtime-protection category using your Volume 3 weighted-evaluation approach, with a recommendation and the evidence you would still want from a proof of concept.

Deliverable (commit to volume4/week4/): a guardrail evaluation report with the measured results, the gateway and policy code, and the build-versus-buy memo.

Self-check

  1. What does an AI gateway give you that application-level checks do not?
  2. Why report false-positive rate alongside block rate?
  3. Why enforce policy outside the model?
  4. Which attack class slipped through most, and what does that suggest?
  5. What would you need to see in a vendor proof of concept before buying?

docs.title: Week 5: Agent and MCP security architecture
docs.text:
Volume 4 · Weeks 5-6: Agent and MCP security, detection and response

You will be able to: give an agent only the authority its task needs, put approvals and stops where they work, and secure the tool layer.

Core concepts

  • Agent identity. An agent needs its own identity, separate from the human's and from other agents. Use workload identities and short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens. When an agent acts for a user, use delegation that keeps both identities in the record, so that the user's own permissions limit what the agent can do on their behalf. This is the main defence against the confused-deputy problem you met in Volume 2.
  • Least privilege per tool. Give each tool its own scope. A "read ticket" tool should not carry the ability to delete tickets. Scope by action, resource and tenant.
  • Tool allow-lists and a tool gateway. The agent can call only tools on an explicit list, through a gateway that validates arguments against schemas, checks policy, enforces rate and cost limits, logs the call, and can block it. The model's request is a proposal; the gateway decides.
  • Sandboxing. Anything that executes code or touches files runs in an isolated environment: a container or stronger sandbox with no network by default, a read-only filesystem, no secrets, and strict CPU, memory and time limits.
  • Human approval that works. Approve actions, not intentions. The approver should see the exact tool, the exact arguments and the side effects, and the approval should bind to that exact request so that it cannot be swapped afterwards. Reserve approvals for high-impact actions to avoid fatigue. Record who approved what and when.
  • Secrets. Agents never see long-lived secrets. The tool layer holds credentials and uses them on the agent's behalf; the model's context contains none.
  • Kill switches and limits. Maximum steps, time and spend per task; a global switch to disable a tool or an entire agent; credential revocation that takes effect quickly. Test these regularly.
  • MCP and agent-to-agent security. Treat every MCP server as a third-party dependency: vet it, pin versions, review tool descriptions on change, and authenticate and authorise connections according to the current MCP specification. For agent-to-agent protocols (for example A2A; check current status), authenticate peers, sign or verify messages where supported, and do not let one agent's output act as another agent's trusted instruction.

Study plan (about 10 hours)

  1. Reread the OWASP Agentic Applications list as a control list and read the MCP authorisation and security sections in the current specification, about 3 hours.
  2. Read about OAuth token exchange and delegation patterns, and your platform's workload-identity documentation, about 2 hours.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 5 hours.

Guided lab: re-architect the agent

  1. Give the agent its own identity and use short-lived scoped tokens for each tool. Remove any shared long-lived key from its environment.
  2. Put a tool gateway between the agent and the tools. Implement an allow-list, argument schemas, a policy check, rate and spend limits and structured logging.
  3. Add a human approval step for state-changing tools, bound to a hash of the exact request and expiring after a short time.
  4. Run any code-execution or file tool in a sandbox with no network and strict limits.
  5. Add step, time and cost limits and a kill switch that disables a named tool within seconds. Prove it works.
  6. Rerun the Volume 2 Week 6 attacks: document-based hijack, tool-description poisoning, privilege test and misleading approval. Record before and after outcomes.
  7. Write an ADR on how the agent's authority is bounded and a one-page note on what an attacker who fully controls the agent's text output could still do.

Deliverable (commit to volume4/week5/): the agent security architecture (diagram and ADRs), code and configuration, and test results for each attack.

Self-check

  1. Why should an agent have its own identity?
  2. What makes an approval step meaningful rather than a rubber stamp?
  3. Why must secrets stay out of the model's context?
  4. How does a tool gateway limit the damage from a hijacked agent?
  5. How do you vet an MCP server before connecting it?

docs.title: Week 6: Detection, monitoring and incident response for AI
docs.text:
Volume 4 · Weeks 5-6: Agent and MCP security, detection and response

You will be able to: decide what to log, write detections that fire on AI-specific abuse, and run an AI incident through a playbook.

Core concepts

  • Telemetry design. Log enough to reconstruct an incident without creating a new privacy problem. Useful fields include timestamp, caller and agent identity, tenant, model and version, prompt and response identifiers or hashes, retrieved document identifiers, tool calls with arguments, policy decisions, guardrail outcomes, token counts and cost, and latency. Decide how much raw prompt text to keep, who may read it and for how long; apply your Volume 3 data rules.
  • Detection use cases. Examples of signals to alert on: canary strings appearing in outputs; many guardrail blocks from one caller; retrieval requests denied by access control; unusual tool-call sequences; tool calls outside normal hours or volume; sudden spikes in token use or spend; model or prompt changes outside the release process; outputs matching known sensitive patterns.
  • Drift and abuse. Monitor quality and safety metrics over time. Sudden shifts can mean a model update, a poisoned data source or an attack in progress.
  • SIEM integration. Send events in a structured format to the security monitoring platform. Write detection rules, map them to the threats in your model, and test them with simulated events.
  • AI incident playbooks. For each incident type, define detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery, notification and lessons learned. Examples: data leakage through retrieval, agent took an unauthorised action, model supply-chain compromise, jailbreak causing harmful public output, runaway cost.
  • Containment options unique to AI. Disable a tool, revoke an agent token, switch to a fallback model, tighten guardrail thresholds, remove a document from the corpus, or take the feature offline.
  • Defensive use of AI in the SOC. AI can help summarise alerts, enrich investigations and draft reports. Treat its output as untrusted, keep humans in charge of decisions, and protect the data you send to it.

Study plan (about 10 hours)

  1. Read your SIEM's or log tool's guidance on writing detection rules, and an incident-response framework such as NIST's guidance on incident handling, about 3 hours.
  2. Review the AI-specific incident categories in your Volume 3 risk register, about 1 hour.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 6 hours.

Guided lab: instrument, detect, respond

  1. Add structured logging to the gateway, RAG layer and agent covering the fields above. Send logs to a local stack of your choice (for example an open-source log and search tool).
  2. Write at least eight detections, each tied to a threat from your Week 1 model. Include the data source, logic, threshold and expected false-positive sources.
  3. Test each detection by replaying simulated attacks from Volume 2 and measuring whether it fires and how quickly.
  4. Write playbooks for three incident types, with roles, steps, decision points and communication templates.
  5. Run a tabletop exercise, alone or with a friend: a scenario where a poisoned document causes the agent to send internal data to an outside address. Walk through the playbook, record what was unclear, and revise it.

Deliverable (commit to volume4/week6/): a detection catalogue, three incident playbooks, and the tabletop write-up with improvements.

Self-check

  1. What would you log for each model call, and what would you avoid logging?
  2. Name four detections specific to AI systems.
  3. What containment options exist for an agent that took a bad action?
  4. How do you test that a detection actually works?
  5. What are the risks of using AI to triage security alerts?

docs.title: Week 7: Enterprise architecture and the business case
docs.text:
Volume 4 · Weeks 7-8: Enterprise architecture, business case and capstone

You will be able to: adapt your designs to a regulated enterprise, quantify risk and cost well enough to justify a roadmap, and present it to executives.

Core concepts

  • Regulated and critical-sector patterns. Banks, insurers, health providers, energy, transport and government have extra duties: data residency, outsourcing and third-party rules, resilience requirements, audit trails and strict change control. Start from your sector regulator's expectations, then add AI-specific controls.
  • Cloud versus sovereign deployment. Options range from public-cloud managed AI, through dedicated or private cloud and sovereign-cloud offerings, to fully on-premises models. Compare on data residency, legal exposure, capability of available models, operational burden, cost and time to deliver. Many enterprises choose different options for different tiers of use case.
  • Reference architecture and landing zone. A reusable, approved pattern that teams adopt instead of designing from scratch: identity, networking, gateway, logging, guardrails, model registry, data controls and monitoring, pre-wired.
  • Risk quantification. Executives respond to money and probability. A simple, honest approach is to estimate, for each major scenario, the loss from one event and how often it might happen in a year, then compare with the cost of controls. State your assumptions and ranges; avoid false precision. If you want a structured method, read about FAIR-style risk analysis.
  • ROI of security. Frame benefits as avoided loss, enabled business (use cases that could not otherwise launch), reduced audit effort and faster approvals. Include costs of people, tooling, operations and delay.
  • Roadmap. Phase work (foundation, scale, optimise) with gates, dependencies, owners, budget bands and a first-90-days plan. Show what you are deliberately not doing yet.
  • Executive communication. Lead with the decision needed, then the risk, the options, the recommendation and the cost. Use plain language and one page of numbers.

A basic way to compare annual risk with a control's cost is the annualised loss estimate, shown below. It is a communication aid, not a precise prediction.

ALE = SLE \times ARO

Here SLE is the estimated loss from a single event and ARO is the estimated number of events per year. Compare the reduction in ALE from a control with the control's annual cost.

Study plan (about 10 hours)

  1. Read your sector regulator's guidance on technology risk, outsourcing or resilience for a sector you care about, about 2 hours.
  2. Read an introduction to risk quantification (FAIR or an equivalent) and examples of security business cases, about 2 hours.
  3. Lab and deliverable, about 6 hours.

Guided lab: target architecture and three-year roadmap

  1. Choose or reuse the regulated enterprise from your Volume 3 capstone.
  2. Produce a target architecture for its AI platform: layers, shared services, tiers of use cases with different controls, hosting options by tier, and how the Volume 1 system fits.
  3. Quantify five major risk scenarios using ALE with low, expected and high estimates. Document sources and assumptions.
  4. Estimate costs of the programme by year, and the avoided-loss and business-enablement benefits. Present the net view with ranges.
  5. Build a three-year roadmap with phases, gates and a first-90-days plan.
  6. Write a one-page executive summary and a six-slide deck, and practise presenting it in eight minutes.

Deliverable (commit to volume4/week7/): the target architecture, the risk and cost model, the roadmap, and the executive summary.

Self-check

  1. How do regulated-sector requirements change an AI architecture?
  2. When would you choose sovereign or on-premises hosting over managed cloud AI?
  3. What is wrong with presenting a single-figure risk estimate as fact?
  4. What belongs on the first page for an executive?
  5. What have you chosen not to do in year one, and why?

docs.title: Week 8: Capstone and design-authority defence
docs.text:
Volume 4 · Weeks 7-8: Enterprise architecture, business case and capstone

You will be able to: integrate everything into one defensible package for a secure agentic AI platform and defend it under questioning.

The capstone

The curriculum calls for an integrated "Secure Agentic AI Platform" package defended before a design-authority panel. Your package combines your work from all four volumes into a single coherent story.

Package contents

  1. Executive summary (one page): the platform, its purpose, the main risks, the recommendation.
  2. Architecture: context and component diagrams, data flows, trust boundaries, identities, deployment topology, and ADRs for the ten most important decisions.
  3. Threat model: baseline from Week 1, updated for the final design, with each threat traced to a control.
  4. Security evidence: results of your attack suite against the final design, before-and-after comparisons, guardrail measurements, and detection test results.
  5. Governance mapping: your control set mapped to the EU AI Act classification, your chosen frameworks and the regional obligations register, with dates and confidence levels.
  6. Operations: monitoring, incident playbooks, change management and model-intake process.
  7. Business case and roadmap: from Week 7, trimmed to what the panel needs.
  8. Residual risk statement: risks that remain after the design, their owners, acceptance decisions and review dates.

Study plan (about 10 hours, plus capstone time)

  1. Assemble the package, close gaps, and resolve contradictions between earlier artefacts, about 6 hours. Expect to take a second week if needed.
  2. Prepare a 20-minute presentation and a list of likely questions, about 2 hours.
  3. Rehearse twice, once with a timer and once with a friend or colleague asking hard questions, about 2 hours.

The defence

The format is a 20-minute presentation followed by 20 minutes of questions. The panel, even if it is only you and one or two colleagues or mentors, is there to challenge. Prepare for questions such as these:

  • Which threat worries you most, and why have you not reduced it further?
  • What happens if the model is fully compromised? Show the blast radius.
  • How do you know your guardrails work on real traffic and not only your test set?
  • Which of your legal claims are most likely to change in a year, and how will you notice?
  • What would you do differently with half the budget? With double?
  • Which assumption, if wrong, would most damage your design?
  • Where have you relied on the model behaving well rather than on enforcement?

Deliverable (commit to volume4/capstone/): the full package and the presentation, plus a short note recording the questions you were asked and how you answered.

Self-check

  1. What is the single strongest piece of evidence in your package?
  2. Where is your design weakest, and have you said so openly?
  3. How would you respond if the panel rejected your top recommendation?
  4. Which earlier artefact needed correcting once you saw it with the others?
  5. What would a reviewer need to reproduce your test results?
